title: Exercise 1.1
text:
Exercise 1.1 (a)
Let \(Y\) be the plane curve \(y=x^2\) (i.e., \(Y\) is the zero set of the polynomial \(f=y-x^2\) ). Show that \(A(Y)\) is isomorphic to a polynomial ring in one variable over \(k\).


Solution:
Here \(f\) is a polynomial in \(k[x,y]\). Polynomials in \(k[x,y]\) are polynomials in the variables \(x\) and \(y\). We can evaluate such a polynomial when \(x\) has the value \(x_0\) and \(y\) has the value \(y_0\) where \(x_0,y_0\) are elements of the field \(k\) to get \(f(x_0,y_0)\) which is also an element of \(k\).
So given a polynomial in \(k[x,y]\), it can be evaluated at a point \(p_0=(x_0,y_0)\) in \(\mathbb A^2_k\) to get a value in \(k\). This process gives a map \[Eval_{p_0}:k[x,y]\to k, \quad g\mapsto g(p_0).\] This map is often called the evaluation map at the point \(p_0\). There is an algebraic way to get this map.
Let \(p_0\) denote the point \((x_0,y_0)\) in \(\mathbb A^2_k\). Consider the ideal \(\mathfrak m_{p_0} = (x-x_0,y-y_0)\). This is the ideal generated by the linear polynomials \(x-x_0\), and \(y-y_0\). We have:
The set of all polynomials that vanish at the point \(p_0=(p_{x_0},p_{y_0})\) is exactly the ideal \(\mathfrak m_{p_0}\).
Proof: Let \(u = x - p_{x_0}\) and \(v = y - p_{y_0}\). Then \(u\) and \(v\) are polynomials in \(k[x,y]\). Given a polynomial \(g(x,y)\) we can write it as polynomial in \(u\) and \(v\), by writing \(g(x,y)=g(u+p_{x_0},v+p_{y_0})\) and expanding the RHS. When the RHS is expanded we get a polynomial \(h(u,v)\) in \(u,v\). The polynomial \(g(x,y)\) and \(h(u,v)\) are the same element of the ring \(k[x,y]\). \[g \Bigg |_{x=p_{x_0},y=p_{y_0}} = h\Bigg |_{u=0,v=0}.\] So the constant term of the polynomial \(h\) is \(g(p_{x_0},p_{y_0})\). Hence we can write \(h(u,v)\) as \(uh_1(u,v)+vh_2(u,v)+g(p_{x_0},p_{y_0})\) for some polynomials \(h_1\) and \(h_2\). Since \(g(x,y)=h(u,v)\), we have that \(g(x,y)=(x-p_{x_0})h_1(u,v) + (y-p_{y_0})h_2(u,v) + g(p_{x_0},p_{y_0})\). So \(g(x,y)-g(p_{x_0},p_{y_0})\in \mathfrak m_{p_0}\).
If \(g(p_{x_0},p_{y_0})=0\), then \(g(x,y)\in\mathfrak m_{p_0}\). Conversely if \(g(x,y)\in\mathfrak m_{p_0}\), then \(g(p_{x_0},p_{y_0}) = 0\) as \((p_{x_0},p_{y_0})\) is a common zero of the generators \(x-p_{x_0},y-p_{y_0}\) of \(\mathfrak m_{p_0}\).
So \(I(\{p_0\}) = \mathfrak m_{p_0}\).
Fact: If \(R\) is a \(k-\)algebra for a field \(k\), and \(I\) is a proper ideal of \(R\). Then the quotient ring homomorphism \(R\to R/I\) gives the structure of a \(k-\)algebra to \(R/I\). In particular the quotient map is identity on \(k\subset R\).
Consider the following map:
\[k[x,y]\to k[x,y]/\mathfrak m_{p_0},\quad f\mapsto \overline{f}\]
As the zero set of \(\mathfrak m_{p_0}\) is nonempty, it does not contain any nonzero constant, because a non zero constant has empty zero set. So the above map is a \(k-\)algebra map and its restriction to \(k\) is injective. Also if \(f\in k[x,y]\), then \(f-f(p_0)\in\mathfrak m_{p_0}\). So \(\overline{f-f(p_0)} = 0\). So \(\overline{f} =\overline{f(p_0)}\). So we can say \(f\mapsto \overline{f(p_0)}\). As the above map is surjective, we have that the image of \(k[x,y]\) is same as the image of \(k\) under the above map. Hence the image is exactly \(k\). Please note here we are identifying the images of elements of \(k\in k[x,y]\) with their images in the quotient. With this identification \(\overline f = f(p_0)\).
So the value of \(f\) evaluated at \(p_0\) is the image of \(f\) under the quotient map \[k[x,y]\to k[x,y]/\mathfrak m_{p_0}.\].
This is how “Evaluation at \(p_0\)” can be intrepreted algebraically.
Fact: Since the quotient of \(\mathfrak m_{p_0}\) is a field, the ideal \(\mathfrak m_{p_0}\) must be a maximal ideal of a \(k[x,y]\).
All these things that we have seen in \(2-\)variables also holds good for the \(n-\)variable case.
Facts:

If \(f_1,\ldots,f_k\) generate an ideal \(I\) in \(k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), then \(Z(I)=Z(\{f_1,\ldots,f_k\})\).
Let \(g(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) and \(p_0=(p_{1_0},\ldots,p_{n_0})\in\mathbb A^n_k\). Then \(g(x_1,\ldots,x_n)-g(p_{1_0},\ldots,p_{n_0})\in\mathfrak m_{p_0}\). and \(I(\{(p_{1_0},\ldots,p_{n_0})\})=\mathfrak m_{p_0}\) The proof of this fact is the extension of the proof given above for the \(2-\)variable case to the \(n-\)variable case.
If \(p_0\in \mathbb A^n_k\), then \(\mathfrak m_{p_0}\) is a maximal ideal of \(k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\).

Note: We have not used that \(k\) is algebraically closed in the above discussion. Hence all this holds for non algebraically closed fields also.
\(Y:=\{p\in\mathbb A^2_k:f(p)=0\}\). Elements of \(k[x,y]\) are seen as functions on \(\mathbb A^2_k\). \(A(Y)\) is the set of functions we get by restricting the functions on \(\mathbb A^2_k\) to \(Y\). There is a natural map \[k[x,y]\to A(x,y),\quad f\mapsto f\Bigg|_{Y}.\] This map is surjective because every element of \(A(Y)\) is restriction of an element of \(k[x,y]=A(\mathbb A^k)\). Hence this map is a quotient map as this map is also a \(k-\)algebra map. If \(f\) and \(g\) are two elements of \(k(x,y)\), that restrict to the same function on \(Y\), then \(f-g\) must be identically zero on \(Y\). So \(f-g\in I(Y)\). The converse also holds, so the kernel of this map is exactly \(I(Y)\). So \(A(Y)=k[x,y]/I(Y)\). Note when we are thinking of \(A[Y]\) as the quotient ring, there is a concrete realization of it as a ring of functions on \(Y\), behind the algebraic object, such that any two polynomials in the equivalence classes given by the quotient map evaluate to the the same value when restricted to \(Y\).
When we say \(Y\) is the plane curve, we mean \(Y\) is the set of point satisfying the equation \(y=x^2\). The equation \(y=x^2\equiv y-x^2=0\). So a solution of this equation is same as the zero of the polynomial \(y-x^2\). So bringing everything to one side of the equation involving polynomials, the solution set becomes the zero set of a polynomials. So studying solutions of polynomial equations is equal to studying zeroes of polynomials. If \(I=(f)\), then \(Z(I)=Z(\{f\})=Z(f)\).
So \(Z((f))=Y\). \(A(Y) = k[x,y]/I(Z((f)))\).
By Hilbert’s Nullstellensatz \(I(Z((f))) = \sqrt {(f)}\). This is an important step.
Fact: The polynomial \(y-x^2\) is irreducible.
Proof:Let us briefly recall Eisenstein’s criterion. It’s simplest form is the following:
Let \(f(x)=a_0x^n+a_1x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n\) be a plynomial in \(\mathbb Z[x]\). Suppose there exists a prime number \(p\in\mathbb Z\) such that \(p\nmid a_0\), \(p|a_k\) for \(k>0\), and \(p^2\nmid a_n\). Then \(f(x)\) is irreducible in \(\mathbb Z[x]\).
Proof:
Fact: For a ring \(R\), if \(\mathfrak p\) is a prime ideal in \(R\), then \(\mathfrak pR[x]\) is a prime ideal in \(R[x]\).
Proof: Consider the ring extension \(R\subset R[x]\). Then \(\mathfrak p^e\) the extension of \(\mathfrak p\) in \(R[x]\) is \(\mathfrak pR[x]\). The set of all polynomials in \(R[x]\) whose coefficients belong to \(\mathfrak p\) is denoted \(\mathfrak p[x]\). This is an ideal. We also have that \(\mathfrak pR[x]=\mathfrak p[x]\). This fact essentially gives us the description of \(\mathfrak p^e\) as all those polynomials whose coeeficients are in \(\mathfrak p\). This is also true for a general ideal \(I\) of \(R\). \(I^e=I[x]\), where \(I[x]\) is described analogously. Note: In a general extension \(R\subset S\), the extension ideals maynot have a such a simple descris iption. Consider the s.e.s (short exact sequence) \[0\to I\to R\to \frac{R}{I}\to 0.\] This is a s.e.s of \(R-\)modules.
For every ring \(R\), there is a canonical \(\mathbb Z\) algebra structure on \(R\) given by the the “cannonical” map \[\mathbb Z\to R, \quad n\mapsto n\cdot 1_R.\] Using this every \(R-\)module is canonically a \(\mathbb Z\) module and every \(R-\)module map is a \(\mathbb Z-\)module map. Hence the above s.e.s is also a sequence of \(\mathbb Z\) modules and \(\mathbb Z-\)module morphisms. The kernels and the images are the same wether we consider it as \(R-\)module sequence or a \(\mathbb Z-\)module sequence. So the exactness of the sequence which depends upon certain equality of these sets also does not change. Hence the above sequence is also exact as a sequence of \(\mathbb Z-\)modules. So the above sequence is a s.e.s of \(\mathbb Z\) modules also.
We Using this the above sequence is (canonically) a s.e.s of \(\mathbb Z\) modules. As a \(\mathbb Z\) module the ring \(\mathbb Z[x]\) is a direct sum \(\bigoplus_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb Zx^n\) of the flat \(\mathbb Z\) modules \(\mathbb Zx^n\). A direct sum of flat modules is a flat module. So the ring \(\mathbb Z[x]\) is a flat \(\mathbb Z\) module.
This is a s.e.s of \(\mathbb Z\) modules by the Eisenstein’s criterion applied to the ring \(k[y][x]\), which is the polynomial ring in \(x\) with coefficients in the ring

title: you asked
text:
Step-by-Step Implementation

Step 1: Set Up Your Offline Workspace
Since you want to write without an internet connection, your entire site will live locally on your machine inside a Git repository. You can use your favorite text editor (like Vim or Neovim) to compose posts in standard Markdown.

Install Quarto and Git on your machine.
Initialize a new blog project locally via your terminal:
quarto create project type website:blog math-solutions
cd math-solutions
git init
To view your blog offline while writing, run:
quarto preview
This spins up a local development server (usually at http://localhost:1313). It dynamically live-reloads and renders your MathJax equations in your browser as you type—no internet required.



Step 2: Configure Native MathJax
Quarto includes MathJax rendering by default. In your global configuration file (_quarto.yml), you can easily define your standard LaTeX packages or macro shortcuts so they are accessible across all solution posts:
website:
  title: "Spec(R): Math Notes"
  
format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
    html-math-method: mathjax
    include-in-header:
      - text: |
          <script>
            window.MathJax = {
              tex: {
                tags: 'ams',
                macros: {
                  \Spec: '\\text{Spec}',
                  \Proj: '\\text{Proj}',
                  \O: '\\mathcal{O}'
                }
              }
            };
          </script>
Now, inside any post, you can write native LaTeX directly, and it will render perfectly:
Let $X = \Spec(R)$ be an affine scheme. The structure sheaf $\O_X$ satisfies...

$$
\Gamma(X, \O_X) \cong R
$$


Step 3: Add the Commenting System (Giscus)
Since your blog is static, you don’t host a database for comments. Instead, you can leverage Giscus, a system that uses GitHub Discussions as a backend. * Visitors can log in via GitHub and reply directly to your posts. * The comments load beautifully on your static pages via a lightweight JavaScript snippet. * To set it up, you just need to make a public GitHub repository, enable the “Discussions” feature on it, and install the Giscus app. Quarto has direct configuration support for this in your _quarto.yml:
website:
  comments:
    giscus:
      repo: yourusername/math-solutions


Step 4: Host Online for Free via GitHub Pages

Create a public repository on GitHub named math-solutions (or yourusername.github.io).
Link your local project to GitHub:
git remote add origin https://github.com/yourusername/math-solutions.git
Set up GitHub Actions to automate publishing. When you push your raw text documents, GitHub’s servers will automatically build the site. You can add a simple workflow file under .github/workflows/publish.yml:

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
name: Quarto Publish
jobs:
  build-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up Quarto
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2
      - name: Publish to GitHub Pages
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2
        with:
          target: gh-pages

Your Everyday Offline-to-Online Workflow
When you are sitting in a library or a café with no internet connection: 1. Open your local project folder and fire up quarto preview. 2. Create a new file (e.g., matsumura-ch1.qmd) using your text editor. 3. Write your solutions, proofread the math formatting on your local server browser, and save. 4. Stage and commit your changes locally: bash    git add .    git commit -m "Finished Matsumura Chapter 1 exercises"
When you are back online: 5. Push the changes to GitHub: bash    git push origin main Within 60 seconds, GitHub Actions will trigger, build the HTML pages, update your blog online, and link any new comment threads automatically.

text:
How Terence Tao Does It (latex2wp)
The default WordPress block editor handles multi-line structural mathematics (like commutative diagrams, custom macros, or aligned proof environments) poorly.
To bypass this, Terence Tao writes his posts entirely offline on his computer as a standard compiled LaTeX document (.tex). He then uses a Python compilation script called latex2wp (originally written by computer scientist Luca Trevisan). 1. He writes and proofreads his post completely offline using a local LaTeX editor. 2. He runs the Python script on the .tex file. 3. The script translates math macros, labels, \ref{}, \eqref{}, and theorem environments into raw HTML shortcodes. 4. He copies that raw text, logs into the online WordPress dashboard, pastes it into the HTML editor, and publishes it.
This satisfies the offline requirement, but it isn’t “real-time browser preview” like StackExchange; it’s compiling a local PDF first.

section: The Modern WordPress Stack (For Free & Math-Ready)
text:
The Modern WordPress Stack (For Free & Math-Ready)
If you want a native WordPress blog hosted completely for free with comments and MathJax, you cannot use the commercial WordPress.com free tier (as it blocks the necessary math plugins). You must use a free host or an alternative deployment model for self-hosted WordPress (WordPress.org).

1. The Rendering Engine (The Math Plugins)
To avoid ugly, unscalable PNG image equations, you need true vector math. You must install one of these free plugins: * Simple MathJax: Allows you to use standard $ and $$ delimiters anywhere on your site. It injects the MathJax script natively, allowing readers to right-click formulas, zoom, or copy the raw LaTeX code. * WP QuickLaTeX: An advanced engine that allows you to define a custom LaTeX preamble directly inside WordPress. This is essential for advanced mathematics because it lets you globally load amsmath, amssymb, or custom shorthand macros (like \newcommand{\Spec}{\text{Spec}}).


2. The Comment System
WordPress has an incredibly robust, native, multi-threaded comment and reply system built into every theme out of the box. No external configurations are needed for readers to comment.

title: you asked
text:
The Major Catch: The Compromises
While WordPress provides a polished UI, it forces hard tradeoffs for your specific criteria:

❌ No True Offline-to-Online Syncing
WordPress stores all posts, categories, and settings inside an online relational database (MySQL). It is not file-backed. You cannot simply save a folder of text files offline and run a command to push them to your server. To write offline, you either have to: * Draft in a separate text editor offline and manually copy-paste when you are back online. * Set up a complete local server stack (like Docker or LocalWP) on your Fedora system to run an entire separate copy of WordPress offline, and then manually export/import the database files to sync them—which is an incredibly tedious workflow for a single math blog.


❌ Subpar Live Math Preview
The modern WordPress block editor (Gutenberg) does not feature an integrated, zero-latency side-by-side math compiler like MathOverflow. While some plugins try to offer block previews, heavy sheets of mathematical proofs with nested fractions, matrices, and custom alignments will frequently lag or throw block errors in the visual dashboard.

objectID: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#summary-verdict
href: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#summary-verdict
title: you asked
text:
Summary Verdict

Choose WordPress if: You prioritize a polished, non-technical dashboard, want a built-in comment moderation system without making users use GitHub accounts, and don’t mind manually copy-pasting your solutions from a local editor into a web browser when online.
Stick to Git + Markdown/Quarto if: You want a true local filesystem backup of all your work, want to write flawlessly in your terminal editor without an internet connection, and want a lightweight setup that scales exactly like a code repository.

section: Design Core: Why This Architecture is Bulletproof
text:
Design Core: Why This Architecture is Bulletproof

Machine loss protection: Your configuration files and posts are entirely plain text (.qmd or .yml). Everything is safely held in a remote Git cloud. If a computer dies, you simply clone the repository, install Quarto, and start typing.
Multi-machine syncing: Git keeps track of files natively. Work on your desktop, push to GitHub, run git pull on your laptop, and your environment matches perfectly.
Zero-runtime client compilation: GitHub Actions compiles the HTML files in the cloud. Your local machine doesn’t need complex deployment packages.

Phase 1: Set Up the Remote Base (Online, Any Machine)
Before installing software locally, prepare the GitHub repository that will host the site.

Log into your GitHub account.
Create a new repository exactly matching this name format to map directly to your personal domain: \[\text{yourusername.github.io}\] (Replace yourusername with your literal GitHub user handle).
Keep it Public, check Add a README file, and create it.
Go to Settings \(\rightarrow\) Actions \(\rightarrow\) General. Scroll to the bottom under Workflow permissions, select Read and write permissions, and click Save. (This enables automated cloud compilation scripts).

text:
Phase 2: Local Workspace Environment Configuration
Because you swap between distribution ecosystems (and even Windows), use a tarball/standalone package approach rather than system-level package managers wherever possible to ensure exact parity across environments.

For Fedora (i3 Spin) & Debian/Ubuntu
Run this setup to safely manage your system pathways without needing sudo rights or messing with system packages:
# 1. Pull down the standalone Linux tarball
wget https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/releases/download/v1.9.38/quarto-1.9.38-linux-amd64.tar.gz

# 2. Extract into a localized application bin
mkdir -p ~/opt
tar -C ~/opt -xvzf quarto-1.9.38-linux-amd64.tar.gz

# 3. Form a clean link inside your user path space
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin
ln -s ~/opt/quarto-1.9.38/bin/quarto ~/.local/bin/quarto

# 4. Bind it permanently to your environment shell path
if [[ ":$PATH:" != *":$HOME/.local/bin:"* ]]; then
    echo 'export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/.local/bin"' >> ~/.bashrc
    source ~/.bashrc
fi

# Verification step (Should spit out the current tracking version)
quarto --version


For a Windows Contingency Machine
If you have to drop down into a Windows terminal layer later, install Git for Windows, then open PowerShell and run:
winget install --id Posit.Quarto
Because your structure relies entirely on standard markdown text configurations, both your text paths and layouts operate identically regardless of your base operating system.

Phase 3: Instantiate Your Workspace

cd ~

Now, construct your key structural config layout. Create a file called _quarto.yml directly at the root level of your math-blog repository:
project:

href: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#phase-4-configure-the-automation-core
title: you asked
text:
Phase 4: Configure the Automation Core
To keep your workflow completely text-focused, you will never build the HTML layout files locally. Instead, a GitHub server runner will intercept your text file transfers and build the user-facing web view automatically.
Create the build action folder paths:
mkdir -p .github/workflows
Create the build file .github/workflows/publish.yml:
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main, master ]
name: Quarto Publish
jobs:
  build-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up Quarto
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2
      - name: Publish to GitHub Pages
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2
        with:
          target: gh-pages
To prevent tracking compiled binary garbage, drop a .gitignore target directly into the project root:
/.quarto/
/_site/

href: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#phase-5-the-daily-workflow-engine
title: you asked
text:
Phase 5: The Daily Workflow Engine

1. Working Totally Offline (No Internet Connection)
Open your terminal inside the math-blog folder, load up Neovim/Vim, and edit your files. To verify your math alignments layout locally, run:
quarto preview
This spawns a local background web instance (http://localhost:XXXX) rendering live MathJax with zero-latency updates directly as you modify text—no network connectivity required.
Once you’re done writing for the day, commit your milestones securely to your local machine storage:
git add .
git commit -m "Completed Hartshorne Section 1.3 proofs"


2. Going Online and Publishing
When you get back to an active network link, fire up a fast sync pipeline:
git push origin main
Within roughly one minute, GitHub Actions will compile your markdown documents in the background. The public will see your fully active site globally at [https://yourusername.github.io](https://yourusername.github.io).


3. Jumping Across Multiple Machines (Laptop \(\leftrightarrow\) Work Station)
Before typing an equation on a secondary machine, open a shell prompt inside that box’s local folder path and execute a pull request:
git pull origin main
This grabs any additions made on your other devices, completely syncing your multi-box infrastructure.

section: Step 1: Set Up Directory Structures (On all your machines)
text:
Step 1: Set Up Directory Structures (On all your machines)
Organize your home space so that repositories belonging to different profiles live inside distinct parent folders. For example:
~/projects/
├── account_one/
│   └── math-blog/      <-- Uses Account 1 settings automatically
└── account_two/
    └── other-repo/     <-- Uses Account 2 settings automatically

objectID: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#step-2-create-sub-configuration-profiles
href: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#step-2-create-sub-configuration-profiles
title: you asked
text:
Step 2: Create Sub-Configuration Profiles
Create two standalone configuration files—one inside each directory structure. These will store the name and email specific to that profile.

Config for Account One
Create a file at ~/projects/account_one/.gitconfig-profile:
[user]
    name = Your Name One
    email = account_one_email@example.com


Config for Account Two
Create a file at ~/projects/account_two/.gitconfig-profile:
[user]
    name = Your Name Two
    email = account_two_email@example.com

objectID: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#step-3-link-profiles-in-your-global-configuration
href: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#step-3-link-profiles-in-your-global-configuration
title: you asked
section: Step 3: Link Profiles in Your Global Configuration
text:
Step 3: Link Profiles in Your Global Configuration
Open your main global configurations file (~/.gitconfig on Linux, or run git config --global --edit).
Append the conditional parameters at the bottom of the file. This tells Git: “If my working terminal path is inside account_one/, merge those specific settings over my defaults.”
[user]
    name = Default Fallback Name
    email = fallback@example.com

# Automated Switch triggers:
[includeIf "gitdir:~/projects/account_one/"]
    path = ~/projects/account_one/.gitconfig-profile

[includeIf "gitdir:~/projects/account_two/"]
    path = ~/projects/account_two/.gitconfig-profile

objectID: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#step-4-handle-seamless-passwordtoken-authentication
href: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#step-4-handle-seamless-passwordtoken-authentication
title: you asked
text:
Step 4: Handle Seamless Password/Token Authentication
GitHub disabled standard account passwords for terminal tasks, requiring Personal Access Tokens (PATs) instead. To prevent Account One’s credentials from colliding with Account Two’s credentials on the same machine, inject your specific username directly into the repository’s remote URL structure.
When you clone a repository or update an existing remote path, format it explicitly with the targeted username:
# Form a fresh clone using an explicit profile target:
git clone https://username_one@github.com/username_one/math-blog.git

# Or fix an existing repository path inside its root folder:
git remote set-url origin https://username_one@github.com/username_one/math-blog.git

Why this works across all machines (Linux & Windows)

When you type git push, Git reads username_one@github.com.
Your system’s native secure password storage (GCM/Secret Service on Linux, or Windows Credential Manager) isolates this distinct lookup handle.
The first time you push, it will ask for a password. Paste the Personal Access Token generated from that specific account.
Your OS will securely lock that token to only match that specific username. You will never have to provide it on that computer again, and your two profiles will never accidentally cross-authenticate each other.

href: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#your-visual-directory-tree
title: you asked
text:
Your Visual Directory Tree
Based on your setup using gits and symlinks, your file system looks like this:
~/gits/                             <-- [Base Folder]
│
├── account_one/                    <-- [Root for Account 1]
│   ├── .gitconfig-profile          <-- (Stores Name 1 & Email 1)
│   └── math-blog (symlink) ───────────┐
│                                      │ (Points to your actual folder)
├── account_two/                    <-- [Root for Account 2]
│   ├── .gitconfig-profile          <-- (Stores Name 2 & Email 2)
│   └── another-repo/               <-- [Pulled Repo for Account 2]
│
└── ~/math-blog/ <─────────────────────┘ (The physical repository folder)

Checking Your Final ~/.gitconfig
To ensure your includeIf conditional rules match your new gits naming scheme perfectly, make sure the bottom of your global ~/.gitconfig file uses the trailing slashes like this:
[includeIf "gitdir:~/math-blog/"]
    path = ~/gits/account_one/.gitconfig-profile

[includeIf "gitdir:~/gits/account_one/"]
    path = ~/gits/account_one/.gitconfig-profile

[includeIf "gitdir:~/gits/account_two/"]
    path = ~/gits/account_two/.gitconfig-profile
You now have a production-grade, multi-account setup that handles your credentials automatically.

objectID: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#what-is-.gitconfig
href: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#what-is-.gitconfig
title: you asked
text:
1. What is ~/.gitconfig?
This is your Global Configuration File. It is written in the standard INI format and lives directly at the root of your home directory (~).

The Scope: It serves as the catch-all, default baseline for your entire machine user account. If a specific local repository does not explicitly declare a custom setting, it inherits the rule straight from this file.
The Role in your Multi-Account Setup: It is the “Traffic Controller.” It sets up your general fallbacks, but its most critical job right now is holding the conditional redirection rules:
[includeIf "gitdir:~/gits/account_one/"]
    path = ~/gits/account_one/.gitconfig-profile

objectID: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#what-is-gitsaccount_one.gitconfig-profile
href: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#what-is-gitsaccount_one.gitconfig-profile
title: you asked
text:
2. What is ~/gits/account_one/.gitconfig-profile?
This is a Custom Supplemental Profile File that you manually created. It is structurally identical to a standard configuration file but lacks any default tracking status.

The Scope: It has zero effect on its own. Git does not scan your file system looking for files named .gitconfig-profile.
The Activation Engine: It only wakes up when the traffic controller inside ~/.gitconfig reads its conditional match requirement. When your terminal is active inside ~/gits/account_one/, Git dynamically injects the contents of this supplemental file directly on top of your global settings, overriding your fallback email and name in memory.

objectID: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#the-cascading-layers-of-git-logic
href: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#the-cascading-layers-of-git-logic
title: you asked
section: 3. The Cascading Layers of Git Logic
text:
3. The Cascading Layers of Git Logic
When you execute a command like git commit, Git queries its configuration values by flattening down multiple text files in a precise hierarchy from lowest priority to highest priority:
[ Layer 1: System Level ]       --> /etc/gitconfig (Applies to all OS users)
           ↓
[ Layer 2: Global Level ]       --> ~/.gitconfig (Your primary user baselines)
           ↓
[ Layer 3: Conditional Level ]  --> Activated dynamically by [includeIf] paths
           ↓
[ Layer 4: Local Level ]        --> your-project/.git/config (Inside the hidden repo folder)
If a setting (like user.email) is defined in multiple layers, the highest layer wins. —

objectID: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#the-effect-of-the-git-config-command
href: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#the-effect-of-the-git-config-command
title: you asked
section: 4. The Effect of the git config Command
text:
4. The Effect of the git config Command
When you type configuration adjustments into your terminal, the presence or absence of flags dictates exactly which text file layer on your hard drive is opened and modified:

Case A: Running with --global
git config --global user.email "math@example.com"

The Effect: This targets Layer 2. Git opens ~/.gitconfig directly and writes or updates the lines under the [user] block. This rule will now dictate the behavior for every repository on your machine—unless overridden by a higher layer.



Case B: Running without --global (Local Repository Scope)
cd ~/gits/account_one/math-blog
git config user.email "hartshorne-solutions@example.com"

The Effect: This targets Layer 4. Git completely skips your global file and writes the setting directly inside the hidden .git/config file belonging only to that specific project folder.
The Trap: If you run this command inside math-blog, it will permanently lock that email to that folder, rendering your elegant includeIf directory scanning script useless for this specific repository because Local overrides Conditional. To let your profile files handle the swapping automatically, you should avoid dropping local directory overrides.

objectID: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#the-final-milestone-secure-token-authentication-pat
href: guide to how I created the blog using gemini.html#the-final-milestone-secure-token-authentication-pat
title: you asked
section: The Final Milestone: Secure Token Authentication (PAT)
text:
The Final Milestone: Secure Token Authentication (PAT)
Since GitHub does not accept your standard account password when pushing code from a terminal, you need to issue a secure Personal Access Token (Classic). This will act as the master key for your randomnumberanonymous profile on this machine.

Step 1: Generate the Token on GitHub

Log into your randomnumberanonymous account on GitHub.
Click your profile picture in the top-right corner \(\rightarrow\) Settings.
Scroll all the way down the left-hand sidebar and click Developer settings.
In the left sidebar, click Personal access tokens \(\rightarrow\) Tokens (classic).
Click the Generate new token dropdown and select Generate new token (classic).
Configure the token:

Note: Give it a clear descriptive label like: Fedora Linux Laptop Token.
Expiration: Set it to 90 days, 180 days, or “No expiration” depending on your preference.
Scopes (Permissions): Check the box next to repo (this grants full control over your private and public repositories, which is required to push your blog code and let the Actions automation run).

Scroll to the bottom and click the green Generate token button.

⚠️ CRITICAL: Copy the long token string (it usually starts with ghp_) immediately. GitHub will never show it to you again. Paste it safely into a local scratch file or a secure password manager temporary note.



Step 2: Push and Save the Token
Now, let’s tie it all together and publish your blog live to the world. Ensure you are inside your local directory:
cd ~/git/math-blog
Run your first push command:
git push origin main
Your terminal will pause and ask you for inputs: 1. Username: Type your literal account handle: randomnumberanonymous. 2. Password: Do not type your account password. Paste the ghp_... token you just copied from GitHub and hit Enter. (The terminal will not show characters or dots as you paste; this is standard security behavior, just paste and hit enter).


Verification
Because you explicitly appended your account handle directly to the remote URL earlier, your Fedora system’s security manager will securely store this specific token linked directly to that specific handle. You will never have to paste it on this computer again.
Go to [https://github.com/randomnumberanonymous/randomnumberanonymous.github.io/actions](https://github.com/randomnumberanonymous/randomnumberanonymous.github.io/actions) in your browser. You will see a green checkmark appear next to your build process within a minute, and your math blog will officially be live and readable by anyone on Earth!
